Albers and Anni emigrate to the United States and become founding members of Black Mountain College
United States / North Carolina
After the Bauhaus in prewar Germany, the Alberses emigrate in 1933 and become founding members and teachers of the fledgling experimental college.
The Nazis close the Bauhaus
The Bauhaus is closed by the Nazis in 1933.
The German art school Bauhaus, which had articulated the unity of art, architecture, and craft, disappears in 1933, releasing ideas that will come back to life in North Carolina.
The Bauhaus closes and Black Mountain opens the same year
The Bauhaus closes in 1933; Black Mountain opens the same year; the two institutions share features of progressive education and experimental artistic practice.
Invitation to Black Mountain College

Invitation for both of them to teach at a newly founded college in Black Mountain (North Carolina), where art was to be at the center of the program and Josef the principal instructor. They cable that Josef does not speak English; they are told to come anyway.

President Hamilton Holt fires Rice, a professor of classics, judging him “disruptive of the peace and harmony.” Rice asks in writing for a list of the charges and a hearing; Holt refuses and declares it before protesting students and faculty.

A professor of classics at this conservative college, Rice is dismissed; the firing of a tenured professor makes national headlines. The president of Rollins yields neither to the press, nor to an independent inquiry that exonerates Rice, nor to the resignations of colleagues in solidarity.
Rice and several supporters are dismissed for fundamental disagreement with President Hamilton Holt's educational policy; incompatibility of character was the real cause despite the official charges.

Black Mountain College founded by a faculty migration

In a footnote, Goodman recalls that Black Mountain College was founded in the early 1930s by a migration of teachers (leaving Rollins College), and that the migrating faculty thereby became the owners of the college, with no board of trustees.
John Rice founds Black Mountain College
John Rice founds Black Mountain College in North Carolina as an educational experiment placing the arts at the center of learning; the school will run for twenty-four years.
Crisis at Rollins College

Conflict over the teaching practices and character of the classics professor John Andrew Rice; several professors dismissed, others resign, many students leave. Questions of tenure and academic freedom; the AAUP sends a committee of inquiry; the affair appears in the national press, making those who left unemployable while awaiting its conclusions.

Black Mountain's founding funds

Of the 15,000 dollars needed to start, the Forbeses (Ted's friends) anonymously provided 10,000 and Ted's parents 2,000. Dreier had promised the Forbeses to give it all up if he did not find 5,000 more; at the deadline he had raised only 4,500 when Warburg, after getting 500 from Mrs. Rockefeller, gave the rest himself. According to Dreier, without this gift from Warburg “Black Mountain College would never have existed.” In the end only 1,500 in guarantees were needed: 1,000 for Josef's annual salary and 500 for first-class passage for him and Anni.

During the summer: a charter obtained from the State of North Carolina, a corporation formed, 14,500 dollars in guarantees subscribed, objectives clarified, an announcement printed, teachers and students recruited, a campus found in the buildings of the YMCA Blue Ridge Assembly near Asheville.
The college opens with thirteen students and twenty-four members of the faculty. First prospectus published in the first year, first catalog announcing the writing seminar.

Meeting Philip Johnson in Berlin
A chance meeting with the American architecture student Philip Johnson, who comes to tea in their apartment and asks them whether they want to go to America; they say yes without believing it.
a street in Berlin, then the Alberses' apartment

The American architect Philip Johnson, an admirer of Anni's textiles, runs into her one day on a Berlin street; over tea in their apartment, he asks whether she and Josef would like to go to America. Without thinking long, she says yes. Anni knows that her ancestry — confirmed in an important Protestant church in Berlin but, as she says, “Jewish in the Hitler sense” — puts the couple in danger.
Rice meets Warburg and Johnson in New York

Rice describes the kind of teacher he is looking for and asks for suggestions. Johnson guarantees “a perfect person if you can find the money to bring him.” Warburg is thinking of Josef Albers at the same time. Johnson has visited Josef and Anni Albers in Germany; although he has not attended his classes, he is convinced that Albers is suited to teaching all students, not only artists. He shows Rice photographs of work by Albers and his students, including wire sculptures and material studies in folded paper. Rice declares without hesitation that this is exactly what he wants.

Opening of the college

The college opens on September 25; thirteen students who left Rollins for Black Mountain join them (the text is cut off after that). The Rollins alumni make up the majority of the student body. Georgia, who settled on site at the end of August, sent out his mimeographed sheets and begged Rice to supply material for a printed catalog; skeptical parents were holding back enrollments.

Wunsch, a former high school teacher in Asheville, staying at the Asheville YMCA in summer 1933, knows of a site thirty kilometers to the east: the Blue Ridge Assembly. Georgia, who has a summer house in Highlands, agrees that it could house a college during the academic year.
